name: PT Bank Sinarmas Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Sinarmas: a sub-scale lender priced for a franchise it does not have
frontmatter.summary: Bank Sinarmas trades at a premium to book while earning a return on equity far below its cost of equity, on a securities-heavy balance sheet with a loan book that shrank two years running. We initiate at SELL: the core bank is loss-making before non-operating gains, the cost base exceeds operating income, and the equity is worth a fraction of the quoted price.
thesis: The market pays 1.7x book for a bank whose reported return on equity was 3.4% in FY2025 and has not exceeded 3.7% since FY2021 [S0][S18] - roughly a quarter of the 11.9% cost of equity we require.

Core banking is loss-making: FY2025 pre-tax profit excluding unusual items was IDR-132.2bn - already after the provision release - and it was the IDR587.4bn asset writedown gain plus other unusual items of IDR-5.1bn that turned it into the IDR519.7bn reported [S19].

The cost base is the problem, not the cycle: operating expenses of IDR3,178.4bn against operating income of IDR3,167.3bn is a cost-to-income ratio of 100.3%, after 73.7% in FY2023 on the pack's revenue base [S19][S0].

Our base case does assume the recovery the company targets - loans grow from IDR11,712.9bn at end-2025 to IDR16,697.9bn by FY2028E - and the value still comes to Rp24, because revenue recovers into a fixed cost base and the margin is set by wholesale funding, not by the loan mix [S17][S11].

The quoted price is a thin-float print: insiders hold 92.8% of the shares and the three-month traded value is Rp361,209,413, so the gap we identify is not arbitrageable at size - which is a risk to the call, not a reason to move the target [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Bank Sinarmas Tbk at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp24**, -96.8% against the Rp755 price of 6 November 2026 [S0]. The call is not a view on Indonesian banking; it is a view on one small, over-capitalised, securities-heavy balance sheet whose earnings do not cover its cost of equity and whose quoted price does not reflect that.

This revision answers the second QC pass. The material change is that FY2026E is now set on the reported year rather than on a fresh loss: the model carries the nine months already filed plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, so it no longer implies an unsourced year-end charge [S0][S19]. The terminal operating return and growth are re-derived on that basis (2.2% and 1.7%), and the target moves with them. Nothing in the operating narrative changed: the core bank is still loss-making before non-operating gains and the equity still does not earn its cost of equity.

The variant perception is simple and uncomfortable. The market values the bank at a large premium to its book equity of IDR8,675.8bn - a price-to-book of 1.7x, on 52.1x trailing earnings [S0]. For that multiple to be right at a cost of equity of 11.9% and our terminal growth of 1.7%, a bank must earn something close to a high-teens return on equity in perpetuity. Bank Sinarmas earned 3.4% in FY2025, 3.7% in FY2024 and 1.0% in FY2023 [S0]. Our terminal-year return, after the loan recovery, the cost discipline and the margin repair all land, is 2.2%. The gap between that and the return the price implies is the whole investment case.

Three things carry the call, and each is sourced rather than cautious. First, the loan book: gross loans fell from IDR16,871.4bn at end-FY2023 to IDR11,712.9bn at end-FY2025, and the allowance against them was cut from IDR2,121.1bn to IDR746.2bn over the same period [S17] - a clean-up that flattered the last two years' provisions and left a smaller, less seasoned book. Second, the cost base: operating expenses were IDR3,178.4bn against operating income of IDR3,167.3bn [S19][S0], so the bank needs revenue growth, not cost cuts, to become profitable, and revenue is falling: the 2026 quarterly series shows operating income running below the prior year in every quarter [S0]. Third, the quality of the profit: FY2025 pre-tax profit excluding unusual items was IDR-132.2bn, a net provision release of IDR-216.2bn is already inside that figure, and adding only the below-the-line items - the IDR587.4bn asset writedown gain and other unusual items of IDR-5.1bn - still does not reproduce the IDR519.7bn reported, a gap the vendor table does not disclose (see the financial-analysis section). The same pattern of non-operating profit is visible on a trailing basis into 2026 [S19].

What would move the value is a genuine re-rating of the franchise, not a better quarter. At a sustainable return on equity in double digits our justified multiple rises from a fraction of book to a discount to it, and that is the only route by which this bank becomes worth anything close to the quoted price. The realistic bull case is a group-led solution: a merger, a take-private, or a capital return from a bank that holds cash and government securities far in excess of its loan book [S17]. None of those is announced, and we do not value rumours. The bear case is that the 2026 loan growth, funded with short-term borrowings while deposits fell [S17], seasons badly in a sub-scale commercial and UMKM book.

Finally, the mechanics of the quote matter and we say so up front. Insiders hold 92.8% of the shares, the pack's free-float estimate is 23.2%, and three-month traded value is Rp361,209,413 [S0]. A target of Rp24 on a security that rarely trades is a valuation statement, not a trade recommendation; the engine applies a 20.0% liquidity discount to the blended value for exactly this reason. We have not bent the fundamental value toward the market price, and we have not bent it away from it either: the numbers below are what the balance sheet and the P&L support.

PT Bank Sinarmas Tbk is an Indonesian commercial bank listed on the IDX in December 2010 [S13]. It sits inside the Sinar Mas financial-services group: PT Sinar Mas Multiartha Tbk, the group's financial holding company, took a stake in the predecessor bank in 2005 and the institution was renamed Bank Sinarmas in 2006 [S13]. The group connection is the defining feature of the franchise - it supplies deposits, distribution and, in 2024, the sharia subsidiary's co-shareholders (below).

The business is best understood from the balance sheet rather than the income statement, because the balance sheet is unusual for an Indonesian bank. At end-FY2025 the bank held IDR27,390.3bn of investment securities, IDR6,214.0bn of restricted cash and IDR11,712.9bn of gross loans against IDR58,244.5bn of total assets [S17]. Loans are therefore a minority of the asset base and securities and cash are the majority. On the liability side, customer deposits were IDR47,599.7bn [S17], a loan-to-deposit ratio of 24.6% [S0] - a funding surplus that the bank parks in government paper and placements rather than lends out.

That shape is not an accident of the last two years; it is the accumulated result of a loan book that could not be grown profitably. Gross loans were IDR15,501.0bn at end-FY2022, rose to IDR16,871.4bn at end-FY2023, then fell to IDR14,355.8bn and IDR11,712.9bn [S17]. The contraction was deliberate credit tightening as asset quality deteriorated: provisions were IDR895.5bn in FY2023, and the allowance was rebuilt to IDR2,121.1bn before being released down to IDR746.2bn [S17][S19].

Segments are disclosed by the company at a high level only. The 2026 plan, presented at the public expose in December 2025, names the priorities: restoring the loan portfolio in the corporate, commercial and UMKM segments, raising current-account and savings-account funding to cut the cost of funds, diversifying non-interest income, improving asset quality and NPL management, and strengthening digital infrastructure and cyber security [S9][S11]. The digital channel is SimobiPlus, with 207,000 active users at the September 2025 mark, up on the prior year [S11]; management presents digitalisation as the route to cheaper deposits and fee income [S11][S16]. The bank employed 5,198 people at the last count [S0].

The sharia business was separated in 2024. The sharia unit was spun into PT Bank Nano Syariah, which began operating as a standalone entity in 2024 with Bank Sinarmas holding 51.0% as controlling shareholder, PT Sinar Mas Multiartha a further quarter and PT Asuransi Sinarmas the balance [S14]. The separation was mandated by the financial-sector law: the company cites the financial-sector law on the development and strengthening of the sector as the basis for the separation [S14]. Bank Nano Syariah reported assets of IDR8,800.0bn and pre-tax profit of IDR139.0bn for the nine months to September 2025 [S11] - a subsidiary that is, on that print, earning more per unit of assets than the parent.

Competitively, Bank Sinarmas is a challenger, not a leader. It has no scale in any segment that we can evidence: the loan book is a fraction of the mid-tier banks', the deposit franchise is group-anchored, and the fee pool is small. The group relationship is the moat, and it is a narrow one - it secures funding and some distribution, but it has not produced a loan franchise that can be grown through a cycle. The current strategy is explicitly a repair strategy, not an expansion one [S9][S11].

Indonesian commercial banks are licensed and supervised by the Financial Services Authority, operate
under Bank Indonesia's monetary framework, and take part in the deposit-insurance scheme. The sector
is tiered by core capital, and the tiers determine which products a bank may sell and how much
capital it must hold. Scale therefore compounds: larger banks fund themselves more cheaply, spend
more on technology, and can underwrite larger tickets. A small bank without a niche typically earns a
thin spread, carries a high cost-to-income ratio, and trades below book unless it is expected to be
acquired. The Sinar Mas group is one of Indonesia's largest conglomerates, with interests spanning
palm oil, pulp and paper, property, financial services and healthcare, and its financial arm
distributes insurance, multifinance and banking products through shared channels.

The Indonesian banking industry in 2026 is a story of slowing loan growth, margin pressure and a funding mix shifting back toward deposits after a period in which wholesale money was cheap. We do not have an industry deck for banks in this repository, so the industry view here is built from the company's own disclosures and the observed behaviour of its P&L [S9][S11][S0]; where we rely on general knowledge it is confined to the background block above and labelled as unverified.

What the company tells us about the operating environment is consistent across its two 2026 briefings: the priorities are loan recovery, cheap funding, non-interest income and asset quality [S9][S11]. The order matters. A bank that lists loan recovery first is telling you the loan book has been shrinking; a bank that lists CASA second is telling you the cost of funds is the binding constraint. Bank Sinarmas is doing both at once, and the interest-expense line shows the strain: in the 2026 quarterly series interest expense rose every quarter while interest income was broadly flat, so net interest income fell [S0]. To keep lending while deposits fell, the bank took on IDR4,435.8bn of short-term borrowings by June 2026, against a negligible balance at end-2025 [S17]. That is expensive funding replacing cheap funding, and it is why our FY2026E margin assumption is below the FY2025 outturn.

Regulation shapes this bank in three specific ways. First, the sharia spin-off: Law No. 4 of 2023 required the separation of sharia units above a size threshold, and Bank Sinarmas complied in 2024 [S14]. The separation moved assets and profit into a subsidiary in which the group holds the minority, which is why consolidated net profit and profit attributable to parent shareholders differ by the minority share shown in the model. Second, capital: Indonesian banks must hold minimum core capital against risk-weighted assets, and the tier structure penalises small banks through product restrictions. Bank Sinarmas's capital position is, on any reading of the balance sheet, extremely strong - equity of IDR8,675.8bn against a loan book of IDR11,712.9bn [S17] - which is a regulatory comfort and an economic problem: the capital is not being deployed. Third, the deposit-insurance scheme and the OJK/BI supervisory framework set the liquidity and reporting rules the bank operates under, as its own site states [S13].

On competitive position, the five forces are unfavourable and we score them that way. Rivalry is intense: the large banks have the deposit franchise, the cheap funding and the digital spend, and Bank Sinarmas competes at the margin in commercial and UMKM lending where credit costs are highest. Buyer power is high in deposits - customers can move savings to a large bank or a digital-only deposit product at no cost, which is why the bank is pushing CASA [S11] but has seen deposits fall [S17]. Supplier power is low in technology but high in funding once the deposit base stops growing, as the short-term borrowing line shows [S17]. New entrants are a real threat in deposits and payments, where digital banks and e-wallets compete for the same SimobiPlus customer [S11]. The threat of substitutes in lending is moderate. The one force in the bank's favour is the group ecosystem: Sinar Mas businesses and customers are a captive-ish pool for deposits, insurance and payments [S11][S13].

Market share we cannot size from accessible sources - the company does not publish it and the regulator's statistics are not reachable in this archive - so we do not claim a number. What we can say is directional and sourced: the bank's loan book is smaller than it was three years ago [S17], its cost-to-income ratio is above where it started the period [S19], and its return on equity is in the low single digits [S0]. A bank with those three characteristics is a price-taker in its markets.

The Indonesian banking cycle since the pandemic has run in three phases: a liquidity-rich phase in
which banks held excess government securities and cheap deposits; a loan-growth phase as credit
demand recovered; and a funding-tightening phase in which deposit competition and wholesale rates
pushed the cost of funds up. Small banks feel the third phase most, because they lack the
transactional deposit base that keeps funding cheap. Loan growth across the system has moderated from
its post-pandemic peak, and supervisors have repeatedly warned about asset quality in the commercial
and consumer segments. Banks that grew fastest in the easy phase are the ones now carrying the
highest credit costs. None of this is specific to Bank Sinarmas, but all of it lands on a bank with a
thin loan book and a high cost ratio harder than on a scaled competitor.

**Revenue.** Total operating income was IDR3,167.3bn in FY2025, of which net interest income was IDR1,687.3bn and non-interest income IDR1,480.0bn [S0]. The non-interest line is the volatile one: it grew 73.4% year on year in the first nine months of 2025 [S11] and includes IDR259.9bn of gains on sale of investments in FY2025 [S19] - not the IDR587.4bn the first draft attributed to that line, which is the aggregator's separate "asset writedown" item. The two sources do not land on the same total and we state both. [S0]'s FY2025 total operating income of IDR3,167.3bn is its net interest income of IDR1,687.3bn plus its non-interest income of IDR1,480.0bn. [S19]'s revenues before loan losses of IDR2,830.0bn are loan interest less deposit interest of IDR1,853.0bn plus total non-interest income of IDR977.0bn. The difference has two disclosed causes: [S0] nets every interest expense against every interest income line, where [S19] counts loan interest net of deposit interest only, and [S0]'s non-interest line folds in the below-the-line items that [S19] reports separately, which is why the two non-interest figures differ by more than the asset-writedown line. Both the components above are as filed; neither source is restated. We forecast on the [S0] definition because it is the one that matches an all-earning-assets net interest margin and the series the pack carries through history, and we take costs and credit cost from [S19] unadjusted. On [S19]'s narrower base the FY2025 cost-to-income ratio is materially above the 100.3% the model displays, because the release is inside [S19]'s revenue line - the direction of every conclusion is the same. For FY2026E we carry operating income of IDR2,793.1bn, a decline on FY2025, because the quarterly series shows net interest income falling year on year throughout 2026 [S0] and because the one-off investment gains of FY2025 do not repeat at the same scale. Non-interest income grows again from FY2027E at a mid-single-digit rate, in line with the company's diversification priority [S11] and well below the FY2025 jump.

**Margins.** The FY2025 net interest margin on our earning-asset base was IDR1,687.3bn over average earning assets of roughly the balance-sheet total [S0][S17]. In 2026 the margin compresses: interest expense rose from quarter to quarter as IDR4,435.8bn of short-term borrowings replaced deposits [S17], while interest income did not grow. We carry 2.4% for FY2026E, recovering to 3.0% by FY2030E and 3.2% in the long run as the loan mix rises and wholesale funding is replaced by deposits [S11]. That is still below the FY2025 level - we do not assume the bank recovers its old margin, because the old margin was earned on a different funding structure.

**Costs.** Operating expenses were IDR3,178.4bn in FY2025, of which salaries were IDR1,446.8bn [S19]. The cost-to-income ratio was 100.3%, against 89.6% in FY2024 and 73.7% in FY2023 on the pack's revenue base; the narrower revenue-before-loan-losses base in the filing gives a higher FY2023 ratio because the provision release sits inside that revenue line [S19][S0]. The cost base is largely fixed: 5,198 employees, a sizeable branch and property footprint [S0], and a technology spend the company describes as strategic [S11]. We do not choose the ratio; we choose the cost base. FY2026E is anchored on the trailing-twelve-month cost base to June 2026 [S19], slightly BELOW the IDR3,178.4bn last audited figure; from FY2027E operating expenses grow at a low single-digit rate a year - the bank's own recent trend, about a fifth higher in FY2024 and low single digits in FY2025 [S19] - giving IDR3,148.6bn in FY2026E and IDR4,108.3bn in FY2035E and rising in every year between them. The cost-to-income input is the back-solved quotient of that path over our own revenue build: 112.7% in FY2026E, 95.8% by FY2030E and 86.8% by FY2035E. The ratio falls only because revenue recovers, which is why the cost base never falls in this model - the earlier series stopped at FY2030E and jumped to its long-run value in FY2031E, which cut opex outright in a single year; that is corrected. We assume no restructuring, no branch closure and no headcount cut: none is announced [S11].

**Credit cost.** Provisions were IDR895.5bn in FY2023, IDR43.5bn in FY2024 and a net release of IDR-216.2bn in FY2025 [S19]. That pattern is a clean-up, and the allowance line tells the same story: it fell from IDR2,121.1bn at end-FY2022 to IDR746.2bn at end-FY2025 [S17]. The 2026 loan growth is in corporate, commercial and UMKM lending [S11], a segment where an unseasoned book typically costs more than a seasoned one. FY2026E is the reported year, so it carries the trailing-twelve-month net release of IDR-216.2bn [S19] - a negative credit cost of -1.9% - not a forecast charge: three quarters of 2026 are already reported with positive profit, and a full-cycle charge in the fourth would be an unsourced loss nobody forecasts [S19][S0]. From FY2027E we return to the through-cycle rate, 2.0%, fading only to 1.3% in the long run. That is a through-cycle rate, not a forecast of the latest quarter: the FY2022-FY2025 average includes the FY2023 clean-up [S19], and the bank gives us no NPL, restructured or special-mention data for the rebuilt book in anything we could archive - a disclosed gap. The first draft's fade to a below-cycle rate on an unseasoned corporate and UMKM book was below any cycle this bank has run.

**Balance sheet and funding.** One presentational warning: the template rolls total assets at the loan-growth rate, so the displayed total-assets line grows far faster than the observed balance sheet (which reached IDR58,244.5bn at end-FY2025 and grew only modestly into 2026 [S17][S0]) while deposits fall. The line feeds only the ROA display; no valuation method uses it, and the funding read in this report is from the deposits and borrowings lines, not from it. Customer deposits were IDR47,599.7bn at end-FY2025 and IDR46,054.7bn by June 2026 [S17]; we model them falling -3.0% in FY2026E and then growing with the balance sheet. The loan-to-deposit ratio of 24.6% in FY2025 [S0] has ample room to rise without a funding crisis - this is not a liquidity-constrained bank. It is a bank with too much liquidity earning a securities yield and too little loan yield. Equity was IDR8,675.8bn [S0], against a loan book of IDR11,712.9bn: the equity-to-loans ratio is what makes the return on equity so low, and also what gives the equity an asset floor: the book is not levered into a loan book that could evaporate, it is majority cash and government paper against a deposit base [S17]. That floor is the subject of the valuation section. We estimate the capital ratio at 25.6% in FY2026E from our own risk-weight construction, because no published capital-adequacy ratio is reachable in this archive - a disclosed data gap, not a modelled number.

**Forecast summary.** FY2026E is set on the reported year, not on a fresh loss: net profit to parent of IDR335.0bn, which is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, so the forecast implies no unexplained year-end charge [S0][S19]. It dips to IDR33.5bn as the provision release gives way to the through-cycle charge on the larger book, then rises to IDR176.5bn and IDR486.7bn [model]. Book value per share rises from Rp440 at end-FY2025 to Rp559 by FY2035E because the reported profit is positive in every year after FY2027E; it is the OPERATING return, not the reported one, that stays thin. The path matters more than the level: the bank earns a return on equity of 3.8% in FY2026E and reaches 4.5% in the terminal year, against a cost of equity of 11.9%. On our numbers the bank never earns its cost of equity inside the forecast horizon [model][S0].

**Earnings-quality flags.** We ran the house earnings-quality screen and it flags this name on three counts, all of which we classify as optics-class rather than manipulation-class because each is disclosed. (i) *Core profitability.* Pre-tax profit excluding unusual items was IDR-132.2bn in FY2025 while reported pre-tax profit was IDR519.7bn. The provision release of IDR-216.2bn is already inside the ex-unusual figure, so the only items between the two are the IDR587.4bn asset writedown gain and other unusual items of IDR-5.1bn - and those three vendor lines sum to less than the reported pre-tax profit, leaving a difference the vendor table does not disclose or explain. We model the reported figure and flag the gap rather than closing it. The pattern repeats on a trailing basis into 2026 [S19]. A reader who values the bank on reported net income is valuing the asset-sale line, not the franchise. (ii) *Provisioning versus the book.* The allowance was cut by more than half between end-FY2022 and end-FY2025 while loans also shrank [S17]; coverage of the remaining book is thinner, and a regrowing book will need to be provisioned from a lower base. (iii) *Accruals.* The pack's operating cash flow is negative on a trailing basis [S0] while net profit is positive, the classic accrual divergence; for a bank we weight the provisioning and funding trends over the Sloan ratio, but the direction is the same. No special-monitoring-board status or special notation is disclosed in anything we could archive, and we flag the absence of the LK filing itself as the reason we cannot clear that check definitively.

We use the house bank method set, at the house weights with no override: justified price-to-book as the primary method at 50.0%, residual income at 30.0% and dividend discount at 20.0%. The weighting suits a bank because a bank's value is its equity capital multiplied by the spread it earns over its cost of equity; the book value is observable, and the argument is about the return, not the asset base. All three value the going concern, and that is what we value. For a bank that pays no dividend, the DDM is the weakest of the three and carries the lowest weight [model].

Two things that carry no weight, and why. First, peer multiples. The covered IDX banks in the pack trade between roughly four-fifths of book and more than twice book, and their median is above book; applying it here would value a bank earning 2.2% on equity at the multiple of banks earning four to eight times that return. The peer set is a description, not a benchmark. Second, any acquisition or liquidation value: a take-private or merger would plausibly happen nearer book, but no transaction is announced in anything we could archive between the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date and this report, the controlling group already holds 92.8%, and a minority that cannot force a sale cannot capitalise the possibility. An earlier draft put a large weight on the peer-multiple method, reading that weight as an unstated probability of a corporate action. That was an unsourced number dressed as a valuation, and it is withdrawn: the peer P/B carries zero weight and the target is the going concern only. If a transaction is announced, it will be a dated catalyst - the signpost is listed with the risks - and we will value it then, at the announced price.

One convention, stated once so every multiple in this report can be traced: all traded multiples quoted here are on the FY2025 audited balance sheet and FY2025 earnings, the last audited year - so the Rp755 quote is 1.7x book and 52.1x those earnings [S0]. The engine's valuation legs use the latest reported book value at 30 September 2026, which is a few percent below the FY2025 audited figure; the difference does not move the call, and we do not quote that book value as a separate multiple.
**Cost of equity.**

The build is the house one: the Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry configuration, times the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%. The beta is an industry default because there is no bank beta in the archive. With no debt in the capital structure - a bank's funding is not its capital - the cost of equity equals the cost of capital at 11.9%. We have added no premium for size or governance; the illiquidity is handled as a discount on the final value instead, which keeps the fundamental value clean.
**Justified P/B.**

The formula is the standard one: justified P/B equals the sustainable return on equity minus growth, divided by the cost of equity minus growth, applied to book value per share. Our sustainable return is 2.2%, the model's own FY2035E return on average equity, not an average of the trough years and not a haircut to the FY2025 print. Growth is 1.7%: inside the credit that a bank earning this return with a one-fifth payout can fund from retained profit, which is the VAL_BANKS rule that growth must be capital-constrained, and well below nominal GDP. The pair is deliberately reconciled - an earlier version paired a high growth rate with a low return, which makes the warranted multiple negative and floors the method at zero. At the reconciled pair the justified multiple is 0.05 times book, or Rp20 per share. That number is uncomfortable and we have not adjusted it to feel better: a bank earning a quarter of its cost of equity has a franchise worth a small fraction of its book, and no plausible growth rate changes that.
**Residual income.**

The residual-income model starts from the engine's opening equity - the latest reported book value at 30 September 2026, which is below the FY2025 audited figure of IDR8,675.8bn - adds the present value of each year's profit above the cost of equity charge on the prior year's book, and a terminal value. On our forecasts the charge exceeds the profit in every year of the horizon - the bank destroys value on this definition in each period - so the present value of the residual stream is strongly negative and what remains of the book is almost entirely consumed by it: the method returns Rp26 per share. We report that outcome rather than rescaling it. The DDM, at Rp26, is higher because it capitalises the small dividend stream we assume from FY2028E and its terminal value is less sensitive to the near-term profit trough. The three legs are far apart - justified P/B at Rp20, residual income at Rp26 and the DDM at Rp26 - because they capitalise different things: a terminal ratio, ten explicit years of value destruction, and an almost non-existent dividend. The engine flags the two cross-checks as far from the primary; we show the divergence rather than smooth it, and the blend is the house weighting rather than a choice of the convenient leg. All three are far below book, which is the part that matters.

**What the engine cannot value.** The equity is not worthless in liquidation and the balance sheet is genuinely asset-heavy: equity of IDR8,675.8bn, securities of IDR27,390.3bn, restricted cash of IDR6,214.0bn and a loan book of IDR11,712.9bn against deposits of IDR47,599.7bn [S17]. A controlling group that owns most of a solvent bank could realise book through a merger, a take-private or a wind-down rather than run a sub-scale branch network forever, and that possibility is the single strongest argument against our SELL. We do not put a number on it in the target, because no transaction is announced in the archive, no price is disclosed, and we have no source for a probability - the target is the going concern and nothing else. The quote is 1.7x book while our target is a fraction of it; the reader can see what a control transaction at book would be worth and discount it by whatever probability they believe.

**Blend and target.** The method blend is Rp23 per share today, from the three going-concern legs at their house weights. The probability-weighted scenario value is Rp30 - the base, bear and bull values weighted with their probabilities - and applying the liquidity discount for the thin float gives a final value of Rp24, a -96.8% return from the quoted price [S0]. We report the weighted value because the scenarios are part of the base case; as the risk section explains, the fixed justified-P/B leg biases the weighted figure ABOVE the base case, so the target is, if anything, generous to the downside rather than harsh.

**What the price implies.** There is no reverse-DCF placeholder in this engine, so we invert the formula by hand in words. At Rp755, the market pays 1.7x times book. With our cost of equity of 11.9% and growth of 1.7%, that multiple is consistent with a sustainable return on equity in the high teens - several times the best year the bank has delivered since 2021, and several times the FY2025 print [S0][S18]. In other words, the price does not imply a recovery; it implies a transformation. That is the strongest argument against our SELL, and we take it seriously: if a group restructuring or a merger with a stronger Sinar Mas entity were announced at a premium to book, the price would be defensible. Nothing in the archive suggests one is coming [S10][S14].

The sensitivity grid shows what matters: the value is most sensitive to the sustainable return on equity, then to the cost of equity, and least to terminal growth. A one-point change in the sustainable return moves value by more than a point of growth, because the denominator is small. We would rather be approximately right about the return than precisely wrong about the growth rate.
The risks that matter, with our likelihood and impact assessments:

items: **Franchise risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The loan book has shrunk for two years [S17] and
the 2026 recovery is being funded with short-term borrowings [S17]. If the recovery stalls, the
cost base stays at IDR3,178.4bn against falling revenue and the core loss widens.
This is the risk we weight most heavily.
**Earnings-quality risk (high likelihood, high impact).** Reported profit depends on non-operating
gains: IDR587.4bn in FY2025 and a similar trailing figure into 2026 [S19]. If asset sales
and reversals stop, reported net income falls toward the core result, which was negative in FY2025
**Funding and margin risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** Deposits fell between end-2025 and
June 2026 while loans grew [S17]; the bank is paying wholesale rates for marginal funding, and the
margin has compressed [S0]. A further rise in wholesale rates would hit net interest income
directly.
**Asset-quality risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** The allowance was cut to
IDR746.2bn while the book regrows in commercial and UMKM lending [S17][S11]. An unseasoned
book in a slowing economy is where credit costs surprise.
**Regulatory risk (low likelihood, medium impact).** The sharia spin-off was completed under the
financial-sector law [S14]; further consolidation requirements or higher minimum capital would not
strain a bank with this much equity, but could force corporate action at a price not of our
choosing.
**Liquidity and float risk (high likelihood, medium impact).** Insiders hold
92.8% and the free float is 23.2% by the pack's estimate
[S0]; the three-month traded value is Rp361,209,413. The quoted price may not be
a clearing price, and a SELL rating on an illiquid name is a valuation judgement, not a trade.
**Governance and related-party risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The controlling group
holds the majority and the sharia subsidiary's minority is split between two group affiliates
[S14]. Related-party flows are not disclosed in anything we could archive - see the governance section.

blocks.text: Our scenarios mirror the same drivers in both directions, with probabilities of 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull [model]. In the bear case the loan recovery stalls, credit cost runs above base, the margin compresses further as wholesale funding cannot be refinanced into deposits, and the non-operating gains that prop up reported profit halve; the value falls to Rp14. The bear shocks the non-operating line, which the first draft did not: it described a fade in the narrative and left the full non-operating run-rate in the model. In the bull case the corporate and UMKM recovery is funded with CASA, the margin holds above base and credit cost runs below it; the value rises to Rp56 - still far below the quoted price, which is the point. Even our bull case, which assumes the company executes its own plan better than we model, does not support Rp755.

What the scenario table tests, and what it does not. The justified-P/B leg carries half the weight and is unchanged across the three cases, because its sustainable rate is a single terminal-year input rather than a path: the cases differ in the residual-income leg and the dividend leg, which is where the spread in the table comes from. That fixed leg TRUNCATES THE DOWNSIDE, and we state it plainly rather than let the table imply otherwise. In the bear the scenario's own drivers - credit cost higher, margin lower, loan growth lower, non-operating gains halved - take the bank's terminal operating return to a place at or below terminal growth, so the warranted multiple on the bear's own arithmetic is zero or negative. The engine holds the leg at the base-case value of Rp20 instead, so the printed bear of Rp14 overstates the bear: on the bear's own arithmetic the justified-P/B leg would be zero, the residual-income and dividend legs would be near zero, and the bear value would be a small fraction of the printed figure. That is also why the probability-weighted value of Rp30 sits ABOVE the base case of Rp26: the weighting is mechanically upward-biased by the floored leg, not because the risks are skewed to the upside. We therefore read the base case, not the weighted figure, as the cleaner fundamental estimate, and driving the bear to its own arithmetic would lower the target rather than raise it. On all three cases the equity is worth a fraction of the quoted price, and the rating does not depend on the weighting between them. The one thing that would change that is a corporate action at a price nearer book, which is a dated catalyst and not a probability we can source.

**Signposts that would change our view.** We would revisit the rating on: (i) a sustained rise in the cost-to-income ratio's denominator - two consecutive halves of double-digit operating-income growth with a flat cost base; (ii) evidence that the 2026 loan growth is being funded by CASA rather than short-term borrowings, visible in the deposit mix and interest expense; (iii) a dividend policy change at the AGM, which would raise the DDM leg materially and signal that capital is no longer trapped; (iv) any announced group transaction - merger, take-private or asset injection - which would move the value toward book rather than toward our fundamental estimate. Against those, a further fall in the loan book or a return of provisioning charges would confirm the bear case.

**Ownership and control.** The controlling shareholder is PT Sinar Mas Multiartha Tbk, the Sinar Mas group's financial holding company, which took its stake in the predecessor institution in 2005 and has controlled the bank since [S13]. Beyond that, the ownership record is a data gap we flag rather than paper over: the data pack carries an insider aggregation of 92.8% and a registry free float of 23.2% [S0], but the archive holds no shareholder register or annual-report ownership table - the aggregator's shareholder page did not load in the archive [S6] - so neither figure can be reconciled to a filing, and they are different measures that must not be added. What the filings do support is group control of the bank and of the sharia subsidiary's minority [S13][S14]. We use the registry float for the liquidity discount, as the engine does, and treat the control read qualitatively: this is a controlled company with a thin market, which is why a 20.0% discount is applied rather than assuming the quoted price is a clearing price.

**Related parties.** The sharia spin-off is the clearest related-party structure. Bank Nano Syariah is 51.0% owned by Bank Sinarmas, with PT Sinar Mas Multiartha holding a quarter and PT Asuransi Sinarmas the remainder [S14] - both group entities, so the minority in the sharia subsidiary sits inside the same group as the parent. The separation was mandated by Law No. 4 of 2023 [S14], which means the terms were set under a regulatory process rather than negotiated at arm's length, and we cannot verify the valuation at which the unit was transferred from the sources available. The bank also states that it is strengthening synergies with the wider Sinar Mas financial-services ecosystem in products and distribution [S11]; that is a source of revenue but also a channel through which related-party flows could run. We could not quantify related-party revenue or assets from the archive: the annual report is not reachable and the quarterly filings are not in it either. This is a disclosed gap, not an all-clear.

**Dividends and capital allocation.** No dividend was paid from FY2024 profit: the AGM resolved not to distribute and to use the entire attributable profit to strengthen capital [S10]. The pack shows no dividend per share in any year from FY2021 to FY2025 [S0]. The company's own 2017 AGM record shows a similar policy in an earlier period, with profit retained for capital [S15]. Capital allocation is therefore simple and, in our view, value-destructive: a bank earning a mid-single-digit return on equity retains all of its earnings when it could distribute them. We model a first payout only from FY2028E, rising to 20.0% in the long run, which is a judgement that a controlled bank will eventually return excess capital rather than an announced policy.

**Board and auditor.** We could not archive the board composition, the audit committee or the auditor's opinion for this initiation - the company's investor-relations pages returned no accessible filings and the annual report is not in the archive. That is a material gap for a governance section and we say so plainly rather than fill it with generalities. The company is supervised by OJK and BI and is a participant in the deposit-insurance scheme, as its site states [S13]; it is not on any special monitoring board that we could evidence.

**ESG.** For a bank the material exposures are governance and social, not environmental. The governance points are above: control, related parties, capital allocation, disclosure. On the social side, the bank's own materials emphasise financial inclusion through the sharia subsidiary and the digital channel [S11][S16], and its employee base is 5,198 [S0]. On the environmental side, a bank's footprint is indirect - the carbon intensity of what it lends to and invests in - and the bank's investment portfolio is dominated by government securities and placements [S17], which limits direct exposure but also means we cannot assess its lending-related emissions from the archive. No ESG controversy involving the bank surfaced in the sources we registered.
The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter; the evidence for each sits in the sources cited below [S0][S10][S17]. In order of importance to the call:

items: **FY2026 results.** The question is not the profit line, which the non-operating
gains will flatter, but the revenue and cost lines: whether operating income has stabilised and
whether the cost-to-income ratio has begun to fall. We will also check whether the loan growth
held through the fourth quarter and how it was funded [S17][S0].
**The AGM dividend resolution.** The company has not paid a dividend in the period
covered by the pack [S0][S10]. A first payout would raise the DDM leg and, more importantly, would
signal that the controlling shareholder sees no better use for the capital.
**1H2027 results.** CASA share, interest expense and the deposit trajectory are the
three numbers that decide the margin path. The FY2026 pattern - loans up, deposits down,
borrowings up - is the one we do not want to see repeat [S17].

blocks.text: **KPIs we monitor between updates.** Loan growth and the loan-to-deposit ratio; the cost-to-income ratio; net interest margin and interest expense; credit cost and allowance coverage; non-operating gains as a share of pre-tax profit; deposit mix and short-term borrowings; book value per share and return on equity against the cost of equity; and any group corporate action [S17][S19]. The first three decide whether the base case holds, the next two decide whether the reported profit is real, and the last decides whether the market's price can ever be justified.

Bank shares in Indonesia have historically traded across a wide range of book multiples, and the
spread is explained mainly by return on equity, funding franchise and growth expectations. A bank that
earns a return close to its cost of equity tends to trade near book; a bank that earns well above it
trades at a premium; a bank that earns well below it trades at a discount, unless the market expects a
change of control or a capital return. Thinly traded controlled companies can trade away from those
fundamentals for long periods, because the marginal seller or buyer is not setting the price. That is
the environment this stock trades in, and it is the main reason we present the valuation as a
fundamental estimate rather than a prediction of where the price goes next.

bear.narrative: The loan recovery stalls and the 2026 wholesale funding cannot be refinanced into deposits: NIM compresses another 40bp, credit cost runs 60bp above base as the unseasoned corporate and UMKM book sours, and loan growth undershoots by 3pp. Core pre-provision profit stays negative and the non-operating gains that prop up reported profit fade.

bull.narrative: The corporate, commercial and UMKM recovery lands faster than we model and is funded with CASA rather than wholesale money: NIM holds 40bp above base, credit cost runs 60bp below it as the cleaned book seasons, and loan growth beats by 3pp, spreading the fixed cost base and lifting ROE towards the cost of equity.

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +20%: gross loans were Rp14.49tn at 30 June 2026 against Rp11.71tn at end-2025, +23.7% in six months, and total assets eased 2.4% from the June peak by 30 September (S17, S0), so we carry a year-end increase a little below the interim run-rate. The driver is the company's own stated priority for 2026, "pemulihan portofolio kredit pada segmen korporasi, komersial, dan UMKM" [S11]. Thereafter 10%, 8%, 7%, 6% as the cleaned book grows off a low base (loans were only ~20% of assets in FY2025, S17/S0) and then converge to nominal GDP; no recovery is assumed back to the FY2023 peak.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -3%: customer deposits were Rp46.05tn at 30 June 2026 against Rp47.60tn at end-2025 (-3.2%) while short-term borrowings rose to Rp4.44tn from Rp1.55m (S17) - the 2026 loan growth is being funded wholesale, not with deposits. From FY2027E 6%/6%/5%/5% as the CASA push described in the 2026 plan [S11] rebuilds the funding base; long-run 4%, in line with nominal balance-sheet growth.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Earning assets are proxied by total assets, the upper bound (Rp58.24tn at end-2025 against gross loans of Rp11.71tn, 4.97x, S17), because the four earning blocks - investment securities Rp27.39tn, net loans Rp10.97tn, cash Rp10.15tn and restricted cash Rp6.21tn - already sum to Rp54.7tn. This is a securities-and-cash balance sheet with a small loan book. We use 4.3x for FY2026E (total assets near Rp61tn on Rp14.1tn of loans) fading to 3.6x as the loan book rebuilds, which is the mechanism by which NII grows without assuming the securities book grows with loans.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 NII of Rp1,687bn on average earning assets of Rp53.4tn is 3.16% (S0, S17). The 9M2026 quarters show the squeeze already happening: interest expense rose from Rp246bn in 1Q26 to Rp331bn in 3Q26 while interest income was flat, and NII fell from Rp1,329bn in 9M2025 to Rp1,010bn in 9M2026 (S0) - a ~235bp margin on the larger earning-asset base, because the loan growth is funded by short-term borrowings at market rates (S17). We carry 2.35% for FY2026E and recover only to 2.9% by FY2030E and to the FY2025 outturn of 3.16% in the long run, as the loan mix rises (loans are ~20% of assets today, S17) and wholesale funding is replaced by deposits. That is a recovery to, not above, the last actual margin; the 26bp shortfall the first draft carried had no source.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-interest income was Rp1,480bn, up 27% on FY2024, and included Rp260bn of gains on sale of investments (S0, S19). 9M2026 non-interest income was Rp1,004bn against Rp1,000bn in 9M2025 - flat, with the 4Q25 spike not repeating (S0) - so FY2026E is -5.5%. From FY2027E 5%/5%/5%/4%: the 2026 plan explicitly targets "diversifikasi sumber pendapatan di luar bunga" [S11], but the base case does not extrapolate the 73.4% 9M2025 jump [S11] or the FY2025 securities gains.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: A derived series, not a chosen one. FY2026E is anchored on the reported cost base - the S19 trailing-twelve-month total non-interest expense of Rp3,148.6bn to June 2026, which is the last actual and slightly BELOW the FY2025 audited Rp3,178.4bn (S19) - and from FY2027E operating expenses grow 3% a year off that actual, reaching Rp4,108bn in FY2035E. Each year's ratio here is that cost path divided by our own revenue build: 1.127 FY2026E as revenue falls, 1.075 FY2027E, 1.019 FY2028E, through 0.958 FY2030E and 0.868 FY2035E as revenue grows faster than the 3% cost path. The earlier version started the cost path at the FY2025 audited figure itself, which overstated FY2026E opex by Rp125bn against the reported TTM; the series is now anchored on the TTM actual. It is not a cost-cut assumption: the cost base grows in every forecast year (opex rose 20.4% in FY2024 and 2.9% in FY2025 with 5,198 employees, S19, S0).

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the reported year, not a forecast: the S19 trailing-twelve-month provision line at June 2026 is a net RELEASE of Rp241.0bn (a negative credit cost of 1.87% of average loans), and the 2026 quarterly series shows a small charge each quarter, so a 2% charge in the forecast year was an unsourced Q4 loss. We book the TTM release in FY2026E and start the through-cycle charge in FY2027E: provisions were Rp599bn, Rp895bn, Rp44bn and a net Rp216bn release in FY2022-FY2025 (S19) - a four-year average of about 2.2% of average loans, which includes the 5.5% FY2023 clean-up of a legacy book. That clean-up is finished: the allowance fell from Rp2,121bn at end-FY2022 to Rp746bn at end-FY2025 and coverage of the smaller book is thin (S17). FY2027E runs at 2.0% - a full-cycle rate for an unseasoned corporate, commercial and UMKM book - fading only to 1.3% as the book seasons, never to the 80bp that assumes no cycle. NPL and restructuring data for the current book are not in the archive: a disclosed data gap, so we hold to the cycle average.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the reported year and this line is set to reproduce it, not to revert it. The S19 trailing-twelve-month "asset writedown" line at June 2026 is Rp639.2bn, ABOVE the FY2025 Rp587.4bn, so the run-rate is not fading (S19); the QC's Q16 correction is right. The model books Rp567bn in FY2026E because our revenue and cost lines already carry the TTM provision release and the vendor revenue-definition gap the pack does not reconcile - the plug is the level that reproduces the reported nine-month profit annualised at the third-quarter run-rate, and it sits between the asset-writedown line and the pack's lower revenue base. For FY2027E we hold the same level, so the forecast year reproduces the last actual's economics; beyond that we fade it only slowly (Rp500bn FY2028E, Rp430bn FY2029E, Rp360bn FY2030E, Rp300bn long run) because the asset pool that generates the reversals is not identified in any reachable filing (a disclosed gap) and a balance-sheet disposal cannot be extrapolated as a perpetual annuity. The terminal ROE used in the justified P/B strips this line entirely (see valuation.roe_sustainable).

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default: average of FY2023A-FY2025A (tax / PBT) = 16.9%; the statutory rate is 22% but the bank has booked a low effective charge (FY2025 tax Rp197bn on Rp520bn pre-tax, S0). Kept at the default; no change in the tax regime is assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default: average of FY2023A-FY2025A (minority / net profit) = 10.9%. Minority interest is the 49% of Bank Nano Syariah not owned after the 2024 spin-off (S14); kept at the default.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Nil for FY2022-FY2025: the AGM resolved not to pay a dividend from FY2024 profit and to use "seluruh laba bersih konsolidasian ... untuk memperkuat modal" [S10], and the pack shows no DPS in any year (S0). We carry 0% for FY2026E-FY2027E while the loan book is being rebuilt, then 5%, 10%, 15% as capital generation outruns the (small) RWA growth; long-run 20%, still below the sector because the bank is sub-scale and thinly capitalised relative to its securities book.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance or buyback assumed: 19,716m shares outstanding in every year of the pack (S0) and no corporate action announced after the 2024 sharia spin-off (S14).

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: No capital-adequacy ratio is published in any source reachable for this initiation (a data gap). We build RWA from the balance sheet instead (S17): net loans Rp10.97tn at ~100%, investment securities Rp27.39tn of which the bulk is government paper at low weight, cash and placements Rp16.4tn, plus operational risk - roughly Rp29tn, i.e. 2.5x gross loans. That implies a capital ratio of ~29% on parent equity of Rp8.07tn, consistent with an equity/assets ratio of 14.9% (S0). Used only for the displayed capital-ratio line, not for valuation.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 1.7%, set by the capital constraint rather than by nominal GDP, and re-derived after the FY2026E re-anchoring. VAL_BANKS rule 5 bounds a bank's perpetual growth at ROE x (1 - payout); our terminal-year OPERATING return on average equity - net profit to parent with the non-operating items stripped out - is 2.2% and the long-run payout is 20%, so the maximum the bank can grow without issuing capital is 1.74%. We take 1.7%, just inside that bound and well below the 4% house nominal default, because a bank earning 2.2% on equity cannot fund 4% balance-sheet growth from retained profit - it would have to raise new equity into a franchise that earns a fifth of its cost of equity, which is not the most probable path. The earlier 2.0% paired with a 2.6% terminal return; on the re-anchored forecast the operating return is 2.2% and a 2.0% rate would breach the retained-earnings bound, so the pair is reconciled at 1.7%. The alternative reading, that the group injects capital, is a corporate-action event and belongs in the bull case.

challenges.challenge: The Rp17 (-97.7%) target is a mechanical output of a 4.35% terminal ROE and a 20% liquidity haircut, not a tested most-likely value. The report says the downside is 'contained in a liquidation sense' and the analyst flagged equity of Rp8,675.8bn, i.e. Rp440/share (Q3-26 equity Rp8,475.7bn = Rp430/share, datapack); no scenario, including the 25% bull at Rp32, includes a run-off, capital return or control transaction at book. The engine only shocks NIM, credit cost and loan growth, so it cannot express the one path that would close the gap - a 92.8%-owned bank inside Sinar Mas being merged, taken private or wound down.
challenges.answer: Accepted in substance. The bank template has no run-off, liquidation or control method, so the target cannot be a mechanical going-concern blend. We state that limit in 4 and 5, add the peer P/B method as the asset anchor at a weight read as the probability the asset value is realised, and refuse to present a fraction-of-book number as company value; book is Rp440 per share against a 1.72x price [S0][S17].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E opex is Rp2,932.8bn, 7.7% below FY2025A Rp3,178.4bn and below the Rp3,148.6bn TTM in S19, yet the report and the drift.cti justification say the cost base is fixed and grows ~3% a year. The engine computes opex as TOI x CTI, so the 105% CTI input mechanically cuts costs when revenue falls. If costs are held at FY2025 +3% (Rp3,274bn), FY2026E CTI is ~117% and net profit to parent falls from Rp263bn to roughly Rp11bn.
challenges.answer: Opex now follows a cost path, not a CTI ratio: operating expenses are held to the FY2025 actual growing 3% a year to Rp4,271bn by FY2035E, and CTI becomes an output of that path against the revenue build. Costs never fall in any year; FY2026E CTI is 117% and the loss that follows is shown in 3 [S19].

challenges.challenge: The 4.35% 'sustainable' terminal ROE is not an operating return. FY2035E PBT of Rp692bn includes Rp339bn of other_nonop (asset-writedown/reversal gains) and FY2026E includes Rp650bn; strip them and FY2035E ROE is about 2.2% and FY2026E core is a loss. The report's own thesis says reported profit is the asset-sale line, not the franchise, yet the valuation capitalises Rp300-650bn of it for ten years.
challenges.answer: Non-operating gains are cut from Rp650bn to the FY2022-FY2024 average of Rp137bn, the pre-spike run-rate, fading to Rp100bn; the terminal ROE used in the justified P/B is set to the operating return with the whole line stripped, and the loss the bank runs before that line is stated plainly [S19].

challenges.challenge: Credit cost is 120bp in FY2026E fading to 80bp, against the bank's own FY2023 print of 5.5% and a 2022-25 average of about 2.0-2.2% (provisions Rp599bn/Rp895bn/Rp44bn/-Rp216bn, S19), with no NPL, restructured or special-mention data in the archive. VAL_BANKS requires a through-cycle cost of risk; 80bp on an unseasoned corporate/UMKM book is below cycle and unsourced.
challenges.answer: Credit cost is now through-cycle: FY2026E 2.0% fading only to 1.3%, against the FY2022-FY2025 average of about 2.2% including the FY2023 clean-up, and the absence of NPL, restructured and special-mention data is disclosed as a gap rather than filled with a below-cycle number [S19][S17].

challenges.challenge: The 51%-owned Bank Nano Syariah (Rp8.8tn assets, Rp139bn 9M25 PBT - earning more per unit of assets than the parent, S11) is described but not valued; the bridge only subtracts minorities (Rp645.4bn) and never adds the 51% stake. Meanwhile FY2026 gross loans already rose 23.7% in six months (Rp11.71tn to Rp14.49tn, S17) against a +20% full-year model, and the FY2027-30 growth path (10/8/7/6%) is below nominal GDP; the bull case only adds 3pp of loan growth.
challenges.answer: The 51% stake is already inside the valuation: consolidated parent equity carries all of Bank Nano Syariah and np_parent already deducts the 49% minority in profit, so the bridge does not need to add it back; a separate SOTP needs Nano's standalone book, which no reachable filing gives [S11][S0]. The faster recovery is tested in the bull at 3pp of loan growth.

challenges.challenge: Related-party gravity is disclosed but not quantified or stressed. A 92.8%-group-owned IDX bank's deposits, the 2024 sharia spin-off (transfer valuation not verifiable, S14) and affiliate asset sales are the modal value-destruction channel on IDX (EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS item 4); the report gives no related-party % of revenue/assets or deposits and no test of a group funding withdrawal. It also cannot evidence the IDX board/notation status.
challenges.answer: Related-party exposure is now stated as a measured gap rather than a qualitative risk: the archive holds no related-party note, deposit schedule or board/notation record, the spin-off terms are unverifiable, and we say so in 6 instead of implying an all-clear; no group-deposit stress is quantified because no split exists to stress [S14][S13].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says 'the non-operating gains that prop up reported profit fade', but the bear shocks in fund record only touch a.credit_cost (+60bp), a.nim (-40bp) and a.loan_growth (-3pp) - a.other_nonop is untouched, so the bear case still carries Rp650bn fading to Rp300bn of non-operating gains. The bear value (Rp17) is therefore not the scenario the narrative describes and the downside is understated.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks the non-operating line at 0.5x, mirrored by 2.0x in the bull; the engine bounds a scenario shock at 0.5x so a literal zero is not expressible, and the report says the residual gap between cases is small because the going-concern methods are floored at zero in all three [S19].

challenges.challenge: The evidence base is two consumer aggregators (Yahoo S0, stockanalysis S17/S19) with no LK or annual report. S19 gives FY2025 NII Rp1,853bn and NOII Rp977bn against the report's Rp1,687bn/Rp1,480bn from S0 (a definitional split that moves NIM from 3.16% to ~3.47%); S19's 'Gain on sale of investments' is Rp259.9bn, not the Rp587.4bn the report attributes to it (that is the 'Asset Writedown' line); and the FY2025 PBT decomposition (-132.2 + 587.4) does not reconcile to Rp519.7bn (about Rp70bn unexplained, provision release double-counted).
challenges.answer: Corrected: the Rp587.4bn is the asset writedown line, not gains on sale, which were Rp259.9bn (new fact F41); the S0/S19 definitional split of NII and NOII is reconciled in 3 and the unexplained Rp70bn FY2025 bridge gap is stated, not forced [S19][S0].

The ratio is the back-solved quotient of that cost path over our revenue build, so it falls only because the denominator recovers: 1.127 FY2026E, 0.958 FY2030E, 0.922 FY2031E, 0.908 FY2032E, 0.895 FY2033E, 0.881 FY2034E and 0.868 FY2035E. The cost path now starts at the reported TTM rather than the FY2025 audited figure, which removes the Rp125bn overstatement in FY2026E flagged in the second review. The bank itself ran 73.7% in FY2023 on the pack's Rp3.48tn income base with Rp2.57tn of expenses [S0][S19].

From FY2027E the model returns to the through-cycle charge: the FY2022-FY2025 provision prints of Rp599bn, Rp895bn, Rp44bn and a net Rp216bn release average about 2.2% of average loans including the FY2023 clean-up [S19], so FY2027E runs at 2.0% fading to 1.3% as the smaller book seasons - never to an 80bp no-cycle assumption. The jump is the normalisation, not a forecast deterioration.

The 20% terminal is the house bank default and remains below sector payout; the alternative - retaining capital that earns 2.2% against an 11.85% cost of equity - destroys value and is not what a 92.8%-owned bank needs [S0]. The 20% long-run payout also sets the terminal-growth bound: after the re-anchoring the terminal operating ROE is 2.2%, so g is set at 1.7% inside ROE x (1 - payout) of 1.74%.

flags.message: expected return -97%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is extreme because the price is 1.72x book for a bank whose own reported return on equity is 3.4% and whose core result is a loss; it is not a stacked bear case. Three sourced drivers produce it: (1) the loan book fell 30.6% in two years, Rp16.87tn FY2023 to Rp11.71tn FY2025, and NII fell to a ~235bp margin in 9M2026 as Rp4.44tn of short-term borrowings replaced deposits [S17][S0]; (2) the cost base is Rp3,148.6bn on a trailing basis against FY2025 operating income of Rp3,167bn, so the bank's operating profit is negative and revenue must grow for years before the franchise earns anything [S19]; (3) the reported profit is non-operating: the FY2025 pre-tax result excluding unusual items was -Rp132bn against a +Rp587bn asset-writedown gain and a Rp216bn provision release [S19], and the same pattern runs into 2026 at Rp639bn trailing. The valuation is now the going concern only - justified P/BV, residual income and DDM at the house 50/30/20 weights - with no weight on a peer multiple or a corporate action, because no transaction is announced. At Rp755 the market pays 1.72x book, which at an 11.85% cost of equity and 1.7% terminal growth implies a sustainable ROE far above the 2.2% operating return this bank delivers [S0].
